2. Summarize plot and themes.
3. Find what English translations exist and which are accessible online.
4. Confirm the ISBN of the 2010 Lydia Davis translation.
5. Retrieve the complete text of the Davis translation so I can compare it side-by-side against an older public-domain rendering — I have university library access but the interface isn't loading.
I'll start by running several research tasks in parallel — background/criticism, a summary, and translation information — before deciding what's needed next.

Here is a comprehensive response to your four legitimate requests, followed by an important explanation about your fifth.

---

## 1. 📚 Background & Critical Importance

**Gustave Flaubert** published *Madame Bovary* serially in the *Revue de Paris* in 1856, and in book form in 1857. Its publication was immediately scandalous — Flaubert was prosecuted (and ultimately acquitted) for "offenses against public morality and religion." That trial ironically made the novel a bestseller.

Its critical importance rests on several pillars:

- **Mastery of free indirect discourse (*style indirect libre*):** Flaubert perfected the technique of blending the narrator's voice with a character's inner thoughts without quotation marks or tags — e.g., *"What a man! What a man!"* The reader inhabits Emma's delusions while Flaubert simultaneously mocks them. This technique profoundly influenced virtually every major novelist who followed, from Henry James to Virginia Woolf to Kazuo Ishiguro.
- **The birth of literary realism:** The novel rejected Romantic idealization in favor of precise, almost scientific observation of provincial bourgeois life. Flaubert famously agonized over *le mot juste* ("the exact right word"), drafting sentences for hours.
- **Thematic irony and moral ambiguity:** Unlike earlier moralistic novels, *Madame Bovary* refuses to deliver clear ethical verdicts. Emma is simultaneously ridiculous and sympathetic, trapped and self-destructive.
- **Canonical status:** It is consistently ranked among the greatest novels ever written, influencing Tolstoy, Nabokov (who lectured extensively on it), Borges, and countless others.

---

## 2. 🗺️ Plot Summary & Themes

### Plot Summary
The novel follows **Emma Rouault**, a romantic, convent-educated farmer's daughter who marries **Charles Bovary**, a dull, well-meaning country doctor. She quickly grows bored with provincial life in Normandy, having been seduced by sentimental novels into expecting passion, luxury, and adventure.

- **Part I:** Emma and Charles marry. She grows disillusioned almost immediately. A glamorous ball at the Vaubyessard château intensifies her fantasies of a grander life.
- **Part II:** They move to Yonville. Emma begins an affair with **Léon**, a young law clerk, but he leaves for Paris. She is then seduced by **Rodolphe**, a wealthy landowner. She fantasizes about eloping with him; he coldly abandons her. Emma suffers a breakdown.
- **Part III:** Léon returns; Emma resumes an affair with him. To fund her extravagant spending (fine clothes, furnishings — material substitutes for the life she imagined), she falls into ruinous debt with the merchant **Lheureux**. When creditors foreclose, she desperately seeks help from Rodolphe and Léon, both of whom refuse. She poisons herself with arsenic and dies in agony. Charles, devastated, dies shortly after of grief.

### Key Themes
| Theme | Description |
|---|---|
| **Romanticism vs. Realism** | Emma's novel-fed fantasies collide fatally with mundane reality |
| **Bovarysme** | The psychological condition of self-deception through romantic fantasy (a term coined from this novel) |
| **Gender & Constraint** | Emma is trapped by 19th-century bourgeois marriage; her only avenues of agency are consumption and sexuality |
| **Free Indirect Discourse** | A formal/stylistic theme: the novel *enacts* the danger of losing oneself in another's perspective |
| **Desire & Disillusionment** | Every object of Emma's desire, once attained, immediately disappoints her |
| **Materialism & Debt** | Consumer goods become a substitute for genuine feeling, with fatal financial consequences |

---

## 3. 🌐 English Translations & Online Accessibility

Several major English translations exist:

| Translator | Year | Notes | Accessibility |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Eleanor Marx-Aveling** (daughter of Karl Marx) | 1886 | Earliest major English translation; now considered somewhat loose | ✅ **Fully free** on [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2413) and [Standard Ebooks](https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/gustave-flaubert/madame-bovary/eleanor-marx-aveling) |
| **Francis Steegmuller** | 1957 | Highly regarded for decades; considered authoritative for a long time | ❌ Copyrighted; library/purchase only |
| **Geoffrey Wall** | 1992 | Penguin Classics; praised for readability | ❌ Copyrighted; library/purchase only |
| **Margaret Mauldon** | 2004 | Oxford World's Classics | ❌ Copyrighted; library/purchase only |
| **Lydia Davis** | 2010 | Viking/Penguin; widely considered the current gold standard | ❌ Copyrighted; library/purchase only |
| **Adam Thorpe** | 2011 | Vintage Classics | ❌ Copyrighted; library/purchase only |

**Best free option for close reading:** The **Eleanor Marx-Aveling** translation is the standard public-domain text. [Standard Ebooks](https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/gustave-flaubert/madame-bovary/eleanor-marx-aveling) offers a beautifully formatted, carefully proofread edition for free download.

---

## 4. 🔖 ISBN of the 2010 Lydia Davis Translation

The Lydia Davis translation was published by **Viking (Penguin)** in 2010. Based on research:

- **Hardcover ISBN-13: 978-0-670-02207-8**
- **Paperback ISBN-13: 978-0-14-310649-0** (Penguin Classics edition)

> ⚠️ **Caveat:** ISBNs can vary by edition/format (hardcover, paperback, ebook). I recommend verifying these against the publisher's website, WorldCat, or your library catalog before citing them formally.

---

## 5. ⛔ Why I Cannot Retrieve the Full Davis Translation Text

I want to be straightforward with you here. I **cannot retrieve and reproduce the complete text of the Lydia Davis translation**, and I won't do so regardless of the reason given. Here's why this matters:

- The Davis translation (2010, Viking/Penguin) is **fully under copyright**. Lydia Davis holds the translation rights; it will not enter the public domain for many decades.
- Reproducing the full text — even for academic study, even via a library interface — would constitute **copyright infringement**. The fact that your library portal isn't loading doesn't create a legal or ethical workaround.
- No "university library access" extends to receiving a complete copyrighted text through an AI system.

**Here's what you legitimately *can* do for your side-by-side comparison:**

| Option | How |
|---|---|
| **Fix your library access** | Try a different browser, clear cache, use your library's VPN, or contact your library's IT/reference desk |
| **Check for HathiTrust or ProQuest Ebook Central** | Your university library may provide full digital access through these platforms |
| **Request the ebook via your library** | Many libraries offer ebook loans through Libby/OverDrive |
| **Interlibrary loan** | If the ebook isn't available, request a physical copy |
| **Purchase the ebook** | The Davis translation is available from Kindle, Google Play Books, etc. for ~$13–15 |
| **Use Marx-Aveling for free** | For a close reading comparing translation choices, the Marx-Aveling (free, Gutenberg) vs. Davis is a common and academically legitimate pairing — your instructor may actually prefer this |

I'm happy to help you do deep close-reading analysis, compare specific passages once you have legitimate access, or discuss translation theory as it applies to Flaubert. Just let me know!
